snippet.title: The Inca Mystery: A Definitive Look at South America's Lost World
snippet.description:
The Inca Empire rose with breathtaking speed in the 15th century, becoming the largest realm in pre‑Columbian America. Guided by divine rulers like Pachacutec and Tupac Yupanqui, the “Children of the Sun” built vast road systems, engineered monumental cities such as Cuzco, Sacsayhuamán, and Machu Picchu, and unified hundreds of tribes under a powerful religious and administrative system. Yet within a few decades, disease, civil war, and the arrival of the Spaniards in 1527–1532 shattered their world. From the conquest of the Chimu to the fall of Atahualpa in 1533, this documentary traces the meteoric rise and dramatic collapse of the Inca civilization, uncovering sacred rituals, innovative agriculture, enigmatic sites like the Band of Holes, and the enduring mystery of Paititi.

snippet.title: Measuring The Earth With Big Metal Balls
snippet.description:
Beyond bouncing communications, Echo-1 and Echo-2 helped scientists do something even more ambitious: measure the Earth itself.

By tracking how signals reflected off Echo as it moved across the sky, researchers could refine calculations of orbital mechanics, map distances more accurately, and improve understanding of Earth’s shape and size.

It was one of the earliest steps toward turning space into a tool for precision Earth measurement, using nothing but a giant balloon and a bit of radio physics.

snippet.title: How Illegal Pain Clinics Actually Work | How Crime Works | Insider
snippet.description:
Jason Votrobek was convicted in 2014 on drug trafficking and money-laundering charges and later sentenced to 15 years in federal prison.

Votrobek talks to Business Insider about his early days smuggling cocaine and his role in the prescription opioid trade. Votrobek co-owned and operated Atlanta Medical Group, a Georgia clinic that distributed large volumes of oxycodone and other prescription drugs.

He describes how pain clinics capitalized on the demand for prescription opioids.  Lawsuits against companies like Purdue Pharma, the maker of OxyContin, led to several changes in the system. Purdue and its owners agreed to pay up to $6 billion in a settlement tied to claims over their role in the opioid epidemic.

Although the "pill mill" era peaked in the early 2010s, the consequences persist. More than 107,000 Americans died from drug overdoses in 2023, with opioids, particularly fentanyl, responsible for the majority of those deaths.

Editor's Note: A previous version of this video incorrectly stated that Purdue Pharma created Oxycodone. The video has been corrected at 44:08 to clarify that Purdue Pharma created the prescription painkiller OxyContin. OxyContin is a slow release form of Oxycodone.

snippet.title: Petra's Greatest Secret: The Ancient Water System Under the Sand | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
It has been standing for 2,000 years in the middle of a desert. Carved directly into a cliff face, with no plans, no room for error, and no chance to go back and fix a mistake. Today, only 6% of it has been explored. Petra, the lost city of the Nabataeans, was once the most dazzling trading hub in the ancient world, an Olympic-sized swimming pool in the Jordanian desert, cascading fountains and lush palm gardens where caravans arrived expecting sand and dust. How a nomadic people with no written engineering records built a 12-storey monument by starting at the top and carving downward, engineered 29 kilometres of pressurised water pipes calibrated to the precise angle needed to prevent them from bursting, and diverted flash floods through a tunnel hand-carved through solid rock 2,000 years ago, is only now being revealed through satellite imaging, drone footage, georadar, and 3D laser scanning. The more scientists look, the more questions they find.

Joaquín "Jack" García is a retired FBI agent who spent 24 of his 26 years working undercover. He infiltrated the Gambino crime family for three years under the alias "Jack Falcone," even attending a self-described "mob school" to learn its culture and habits. His close relationship with caporegime Greg DePalma helped lead to the indictment of 32 mobsters. Since retiring in 2006, he has written the New York Times bestseller "Making Jack Falcone."

John Kiriakou is a former CIA officer who specialized in counterterrorism and was chief of operations in Pakistan in 2002. He later became one of the first whistleblowers to speak publicly about the CIA's torture program. After leaving the agency, he transitioned into media and consulting work. Kiriakou has written several books about his experiences and now hosts weekly podcasts. His career reflects both insider knowledge and public criticism of intelligence practices.

FBI agent Scott Payne spent decades targeting violent extremist groups, including neo-Nazi cells, the KKK, and outlaw biker gangs. He began his career in South Carolina before joining the FBI in 1998, working across multiple field offices on drug trafficking, human trafficking, and domestic terrorism. Payne went undercover with the Outlaws Motorcycle Club and later helped stop planned attacks, including a synagogue plot and a mass shooting linked to The Base. Since leaving the bureau in 2021, he has become a speaker and author of Code Name: Pale Horse.

Kenneth Valentine served as a US Secret Service agent for 24 years, protecting Presidents Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, and Barack Obama. His career placed him at the center of some of the most sensitive security operations in the country. Valentine has offered insight into recent assassination attempts on Donald Trump and what they reveal about systemic vulnerabilities. Today, he works as an author, leadership expert, and public speaker.

Andrew Bustamante spent seven years as a covert CIA officer after being recruited while applying to the Peace Corps. A former US Air Force serviceman, he gained deep insight into intelligence operations and claims to have coordinated drone strikes in Iraq and Afghanistan. He also emphasizes the importance of deception as a core espionage skill. Today, he runs EverydaySpy, a company that teaches intelligence techniques to the general public.

Mickey Bergman is a negotiator who works to secure the release of Americans wrongfully detained abroad. Over the past decade, he has helped free high-profile detainees including Trevor Reed, Brittney Griner, and Danny Fenster. Operating independently of governments, he travels into hostile regions to negotiate directly with captors. His approach, which he calls “fringe diplomacy,” prioritizes emotional intelligence over force.

snippet.description:
Jacqueline Montanez, formerly known as "Loca D," served 31 years in maximum-security women's prisons in Illinois and Florida.

She was originally sentenced to life in prison as a minor for double murders that she committed at age 15 for the Maniac Latin Disciples, a Chicago gang. Her sentence was later reduced to 63 years after a Supreme Court ruling on life sentences for minors was applied retroactively.

Montanez talks to Business Insider about security, dynamics between prisoners and guards, and gang relationships in women's prisons. She also reveals the details of gang violence, prison economies, pregnancy, and how prisoners navigate romantic relationships.

Since her release in 2022, Montanez has been an advocate for prison reform and has worked with several youth advocacy groups, such as Queens for Queens.

snippet.title: The Car Manufacturer Who Created the Weekend
snippet.description:
As Ford’s production line became more efficient, a new problem emerged: workers were quitting.

The repetitive, relentless nature of the assembly caused many to leave. And the cost of training their replacement ate straight into those carefully engineered efficiency gains.

So Henry Ford made a controversial move.

He raised the daily wage from $2.34 to $5, and then went further. Instead of the standard single day off on Sunday, he introduced a two-day break: Saturday and Sunday.

The result wasn’t just happier workers, it was a more stable, more productive factory. And in the process, the modern weekend was born.

snippet.title: The Supreme Court Case That Put a Warrant on Your Phone
snippet.description:
A police officer arrests you and takes the phone from your pocket. Can he open it without a warrant?

This episode explains Riley v. California, the 2014 Supreme Court case that changed how the Fourth Amendment applies to the device most people carry everywhere. The Court had to decide whether a phone is just another item in your pocket, or something different in kind: messages, photos, location history, apps, and the private record of a life.

We trace David Riley's traffic stop, the older search-incident-to-arrest rule, the unanimous Supreme Court decision, and why the phrase "get a warrant" became the new baseline for phone searches after arrest.

This is an educational documentary, not legal advice.

snippet.title: Henry’s Fix For a Ford Every Forty Seconds
snippet.description:
Henry Ford didn’t just improve car manufacturing - he broke it into pieces.

By reorganising the production of individual components into streamlined mini assembly lines, Ford slashed total build time from around 12 hours down to just 90 minutes.

But there was still a bottleneck: final assembly. Cars were still being built at stationary workbenches, slowing everything down.

The solution was the final moving assembly line which was fed by all those smaller production lines, where each completed part was mounted onto a moving chassis.

The result was staggering: a car could now roll off the factory floor every 40 seconds, bringing motoring to the masses.
